contests.title: Ballot Measure No.2 — 24ESEG - An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked-Choice General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws

provenance.quote:
Ballot Measure No.2
24ESEG - An Act Restoring
Political Party Primaries,
Ending Ranked-Choice
General Elections, and
Repealing Recent Campaign
Finance Laws
This act would get rid of open primary elections,
where all candidates appear on one ballot. It would
also get rid of ranked-choice general elections. It
would bring back political party primaries and
single-choice general elections. It would also repeal
certain campaign finance rules that were added by
a 2020 ballot measure.
Elections would occur as they did before open
primaries and ranked choice voting. In the primary
election, voters would choose a party’s ballot,
unless prohibited by the party’s bylaws. They would
only vote for candidates on that ballot. The winning
candidate from each primary would be the party’s
nominee. In the general election, voters would vote
for only one candidate in each race. The candidate
with the most votes would win. Party petitions,
special runoff elections, and other processes would
return. Candidates for governor and lieutenant
governor would run separately in political party
primaries and then together in the general election.
This act would also repeal campaign finance rules
that were passed in 2020. It would remove the
limits on donations to joint campaigns for governor
and lieutenant governor. It would remove limits and
disclosure rules under current law, including for
digital ads, out-of-state donations, undisclosed
donations, and the true source of donations. It
would change the meaning of a campaign
expenditure and remove some fines.
Should this initiative become law?

contests.title: Ballot Measure No.3 — 25USCV - An Act Addressing Voter Qualification

provenance.quote:
Ballot Measure No.3
25USCV - An Act Addressing
Voter Qualification
Alaska law requires that someone must be a United
States citizen and meet other requirements to vote.
This act would specify that only those who are
United States citizens and meet the other
requirements may vote. This act would not change
the requirements to vote.
Should this initiative become law?

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would replace Alaska’s open primary and ranked-choice general elections with political party primaries and general elections in which each voter chooses one candidate and the candidate with the most votes wins. In a primary, voters would choose a party ballot, subject to that party’s rules, and vote only for candidates on it; each primary winner would become that party’s nominee. Party petitions and special runoff elections would return. Governor and lieutenant governor candidates would run separately in party primaries and together in the general election. The measure would also repeal campaign finance provisions adopted in 2020: donation limits for joint governor–lieutenant governor campaigns; limits and disclosure rules covering digital ads, out-of-state and undisclosed donations, and donations’ true sources. It would change the definition of a campaign expenditure and remove some fines.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would enact these changes to elections and campaign finance, including ending open primaries and ranked-choice general elections.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this initiative’s changes to Alaska’s election system and campaign finance laws.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change Alaska’s voter-qualification law to say that only people who are United States citizens and meet the other existing requirements may vote. The official ballot summary says this would not change the requirements to vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would add this “only” United States citizens wording to the voter-qualification law, while keeping the existing voting requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would leave the voter-qualification law unchanged by this initiative.
